newsitem.title: USA: United Airlines mulls regional jet purchase - union.
newsitem.headline: United Airlines mulls regional jet purchase - union.

text.p: United Airlines may purchase about 25 regional jets that would feed its hub operations and add service to smaller markets, United's pilots union said.

The pilots and the company are considering whether United would purchase and operate the planes itself or whether United's commuter airline affliates would own and fly the planes, said Kevin Dohm, a spokesman for the Air Line Pilots Association.

Regional jet flying has become a contentious issue throughout the airline industry. Several carriers see regional jets as an inexpensive way to compete with low-cost start-up carriers. The 50-seat commuter jets are less costly to operate and staff and are more flexible in serving smaller markets.

The regional jet issue has been a main obstacle in the talks between AMR Corp's American Airlines and its pilots. At issue is whether American's pilots union will fly the new commuter jets American plans to buy for its regional airline, American Eagle, or whether the planes would be flown by Eagle pilots, who earn substantionally less than the main unit pilots.
United, a unit of UAL Corp, has identified several short-haul routes which would be served by the regional jets, the pilots union said.
The United pilots said they expected the airline to make a decision "soon," but declined to set a more specific time frame.
"We don't want to debate this issue for so long that we're forced into doing something that isn't exactly what we want," Dohm said.
United Airlines officials could not be reached for comment.
The regional jet venture raises several complicated issues, Dohm said.
If United buys the planes, United's pilots would be paid less than the main line pilots. The pilots' pay is based on the size and speed of the aircraft.
United's flight attendants and mechanics, however, would retain their regular wages. This would make it very costly for United to own and operate the regional jets, Dohm said.
"It may be difficult for United to get the cost structure in line to fly them," Dohm said.
The pilots union said they would be supportive of United buying the jets, but many issues would need to be resolved.
"The pilots are a highly educated group. We understand the realities of the business world," said Dohm. "The pilots understand the the need for different pay scales on different flights," Dohm said.
The pilots, as employee-owners of United, must look at the bigger picture, Dohm said.

The other option is to have the regional airlines buy the commuter jets. United currently has several commuter airlines that operate under the United Express name. These small airlines are not owned by United, but use the brand name under a marketing agreement.
But having the regional airlines purchase the planes raises a series of other concerns, Dohm said.

If the small airlines buy the jets, they may get large enough that someday they no longer need their United affiliation. These carriers could then serve smaller routes on their own, diverting passengers away from United.
A conflict would also arise if the commuter airlines began flying the regional jets on routes United already flies.
United can not "give away" routes to its commuter affiliates unless they can prove to the unions that it is financially necessary.
The pilots union said it has created a committee that will discuss with management the various options for the regional jets.
